type: "page"
title: "Biosensor"
---

<a id="3fdd65dd82be80359477e04d64399077" />Our overarching goal was to develop biosensor strains capable of detecting the presence of antibiotics through stress-responsive reporter systems that generate a fluorescent signal. Specifically, our experiments generated and characterized the CpxP and RecA biosensor strains, as well as produced OD₆₀₀  calibration curves to normalize fluorescent measurements from our biosensor readouts.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be80c79ecfd36364e544c1" />To achieve these objectives, we transformed EPI300 *E. coli* with the CpxP and RecA reporter plasmids. To characterize the growth kinetics and baseline GFP expression of our engineered strains, we performed a growth curve experiment. Subsequently, to determine a subinhibitory range of antibiotics for our biosensors, we performed a minimal inhibitory concentrations (MIC) assay. These results narrowed down an optimal antibiotic concentration range to validate the the GFP expression sensitivity of our biosensor strains.

<a id="3fad65dd82be80e8b091e62bdeac1a4f" />

<Img url="https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/19aac0dddbfc57f792d6d6389a0b216e.avif" alt="" scale={0} align="center" />

<br id="3fad65dd82be80f4b5dbd628ae8788ed" />

# <a id="3fad65dd82be802e8b2ae06e4c514213" />**Biosensor Constructs**

<a id="3fdd65dd82be80a78313caf68bfa742c" />Both reporter plasmids were constructed using the pSB1C3\_J04450 backbone, which provides chloramphenicol (Cm) resistance for selection. Alternative selectable markers, such as ampicillin or kanamycin resistance, would not be compatible with our intended applications as they confer resistance to β-lactam and aminoglycoside antibiotics, respectively.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be8057b500f4b038cdf605" />To linearize this backbone for the insertion of our reporter [Parts](/ubc-vancouver/wet-lab/parts), the EcoRI and PstI restriction enzymes were selected for downstream HiFi assembly. This confers the ability to express superfolder GFP (sfGFP) when the cell experiences antibioitc-related stress, particularly cell wall stress with the CpxP reporter construct and DNA damage with the RecA reporter construct.

# <a id="3fad65dd82be80178e5af6c8962dca2f" />Characterization

## <a id="3fad65dd82be8083ab32c2c0a5db3547" />**Growth Curve Experiment**

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80abaa68f60c95e8f830" />To begin, we generated growth curves biosensor strains in the absence of target antibiotic stimulus. The spectrophotometric results demonstrated substantially higher basal GFP expression in the CpxP reporter strain relative to both the WT and RecA reporter strains, nearly 18-20 fold higher after 25 hours. Additionally, the maximum densities for bacterial growth for the biosensor strains were approximately 35% lower than WT. These differences may reflect a degree of stress associated with the plasmid or the Cm media used.

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80c68481ee431536735e" />

<Img url="https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/62d620975a32525abb0fbdee6731c421.avif" alt="" scale={0} align="center" />

<a id="3fcd65dd82be801ea039e46ebd4e61d6" />**Figure 1.** Normalized OD values throughout 25 hours of growth, at 37˚C (left) or room temperature (right).

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80808778f667aca2f070" />

<Img url="https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/955faa044e7659419f85aa678f904f16.avif" alt="" scale={0} align="center" />

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80e389c1dd17af4c6744" />**Figure 2.** Normalized fluorescence intensity values throughout 25 hours of growth, at 37˚C (left) or room temperature (right).

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80f1836dfc9d65333c73" />We also performed plasmid retention tests to study whether the transformed plasmids are stably retained. This was completed by plating biosensor strains and WT bacteria in various concentrations of Cm-LB plates. The result of these experiments showed that it was essential to have Cm selection pressure to retain our plasmids. We used this in our DBTL workflow to improve our ongoing MIC titration experiments, including using better data normalization informed by the base fluorescence we observed.

## <a id="3fad65dd82be8079befbc4c2621d5550" />**Plasmid Retention Experiment**

<a id="3fad65dd82be8078986aceb67f09dcd2" />To determine whether Cm selection could be removed during the biosensor experiments, we tested how long the CpxP and RecA strains could retain their reporter plasmids after transfer into Cm-free LB. Removing Cm would be useful for removing the confounding effect that it has on the bacterial stress response, but requiring that the biosensor plasmids remained stable without selection.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be80dcb28ee7850aaeb746" />To test plasmid stability, CpxP and RecA cultures were grown with or without Cm for up to two hours then plated on LB-Cm agar plates. Because the reporter plasmids confer Cm resistance, growth on LB-Cm plates indicated plasmid retention, while WT EPI300 served as a negative control.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be803e9904e4dd89054d4e" />As expected, biosensor strains maintained in LB-Cm grew on LB-Cm plates while WT EPI300 did not. In contrast, biosensors grown without Cm showed no detectable growth after one hour, indicating they rapidly lose their plasmid. These results demonstrated that Cm selection was necessary to maintain the biosensor construct during the experiment, despite its potential influence on the bacterial stress response.

## <a id="3fad65dd82be807eb8b0d73c3d0f68ec" />**MIC Titration Experiments**

<a id="3fad65dd82be804bae28fbbe65507270" />Before characterizing fluorescence responses, we need to determine the antibiotic concentrations that inhibited growth of the CpxP and RecA biosensor strains. Establishing the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was important because it identifies the concentration range in which the biosensor could remain viable while still experiencing antibiotic stress, so that we can select sub-inhibitory concentrations to later determine the relationship between fluorescence response and antibiotic concentrations.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be80d9821fdb90bd390f41" />To estimate the MIC, CpxP and RecA were exposed ot two-fold serial dilutions of gentamicin, tobramycin, and amoxicillin, and growth after approximately 24 hours was assessed using OD600.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be80919526e64a35ba1a54" />Across the three antibiotic concentrations tested, both biosensor strains showed provisional MIC ranges from approximately 4-8 µg/ml. This range was then used to guide later biosensor titration experiments investigating whether sub-inhibitory antibiotic exposure could produce a measurable fluorescent stress response.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be808eaceedb8164fbbd5c" />

<Img url="https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/61623405c6d95ca686f2d530bda5cd87.avif" alt="" scale={0} align="center" />

# <a id="3fad65dd82be80c5a420c96e1b62a059" />Validation

## <a id="3fad65dd82be80ffbc1cc433e0f4077f" />**Dose Response Titration Experiments**

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80a4a3e9e5025502b1e2" />In order to build the in-house CpxP and RecA biosensors, we needed a method to measure their responses to antibiotic stress and their growth over time. We used two measurements: 1) superfolder GFP fluorescence and 2) optical density at 600nm (OD600). Fluorescence served as the primary output to measure stress-response activation. However, fluorescence cannot be interpreted independently since the number of viable cells is confounding. By normalizing fluorescence to optical density (OD), a measurement of cell density, we could normalize increase in fluorescence against population.

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80d6bd55d9959a5734dd" />

<Img url="https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/890b8da197df57c49f58189cf046534d.avif" alt="" scale={0} align="center" />

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80e18193c2c8c961772a" />Our first experiments screened a wide range of antibiotic concentrations to determine an optimal concentration window at which CpxP and RecA produced a detectable fluorescent response. We therefore expanded the concentration ranges, and examined antibiotic concentrations, biosensor strain, exposure time, and bacterial density to identify conditions that could generate a measurable signal. For these experiments, we exposed both biosensors to gentamicin, kanamycin, amoxicillin, and cephalexin.

<a id="3fcd65dd82be8045881ef9a00a9eb8fa" />Our initial characterization did not produce a statistically significant response across every antibiotic and biosensor combination. Some conditions showed potential concentration-dependent differences, particularly for RecA exposed to aminoglycosides, while other conditions showed overlapping fluorescence responses that could not clearly be distinguished apart. Because of this, we treated the identified ranges from these experiments as preliminary and repeated experiments before moving forward.

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80859b03e37cb444662a" />

<Img url="https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/220cc0f2bcd95ca595160d5df2c62a7e.avif" alt="" scale={0} align="center" />

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80eea501d24d515d5bd4" />**Figure 6**. Fluorescence intensity relative to the untreated growth controls across concentration titrations.

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80f4a8c1c49bb96416e3" />Future broad screening experiments allowed us to narrow down the conditions tested in later-dose response experiments and ultimately informed the design of our factorial design approach, where variables like starting OD, antibiotic concentration, and exposure time could be assessed more systematically.

<a id="3fdd65dd82be800c87eae5677662dd9e" />The greater goal of this characterization was to determine whether fluorescence from our CpxP and RecA biosensors could eventually serve as meaningful indicators of bacterial response to antibiotics. Although preliminary experiments did not produce consistent dose-response relationships across every conditions, they established experimental conditions and limitations of our system and provided a foundation for future optimization towards our rapid antibiotic susceptibility testing platform.

<br id="3fcd65dd82be807cb1f5c4189b0a5cc8" />
